analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-style health plan covering every American child, plus minimum wage, tax credit, housing, and gun safety measures.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to seven House committees the day it was introduced and never received a vote in any committee or chamber before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a single, very large bill that bundled many separate children's programs: a new 'MediKids' program that automatically enrolls every child born after 2004 in Medicare-like health coverage; letting families of disabled children buy into Medicaid; tobacco marketing restrictions aimed at kids; gun show background checks and child safety locks; a higher minimum wage; a larger, refundable child tax credit and earned income tax credit; expanded food stamps; housing vouchers and an affordable housing trust fund; more child care and Head Start funding; and paid family leave. It never moved after being sent to seven committees.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, uninsured children would have been automatically covered by a public health plan modeled on Medicare, with no cost-sharing for families below 150% of the poverty line and a sliding-scale premium capped at 5% of income for others. Disabled children's families could buy Medicaid coverage; low-wage workers would get a higher minimum wage and livable wages on federal contracts; working families would get larger child and earned income tax credits; families on welfare would keep food stamps and get expanded child support; low-income renters would get new housing vouchers; and parents would get expanded family leave and more child care and Head Start seats.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured children and low-income working families

how_it_helps.text: Creates the MediKids program, automatically enrolling every child born after December 31, 2004 in a Medicare-modeled health plan that follows the child across state lines, with Medicare and Medicaid core benefits including prescription drugs.

Expands Medicaid and SCHIP eligibility to children in families up to 300% of the poverty line on a sliding-scale buy-in, gives states the option to cover legal immigrant children and pregnant women, and lets families of disabled children purchase Medicaid coverage.
Raises the federal minimum wage on a graduated schedule and requires a poverty-level living wage for employees under federal contracts.
Expands the child tax credit and makes it partially refundable, increases the earned income tax credit for married couples and larger families, and extends the dependent care credit to respite care.
Restores food stamp benefits for qualified legal immigrants, prevents hunger among families with children, and creates a national affordable housing trust fund and rental assistance voucher program.

Extends family and medical leave to employers with 25 or more employees, funds paid parental leave demonstrations, and expands child care provider grants, scholarships, and Head Start funding for infants and toddlers.
Gives the FDA authority over tobacco products and restricts tobacco marketing, advertising, and youth access, and extends Brady background checks to gun shows and requires child handgun safety locks.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would fund the grants and the share of MediKids costs not covered by premiums; the bill deferred the long-term revenue plan to a Treasury report on 'progressive tax changes.' Families above 150% of poverty would pay a sliding-scale MediKids premium through their tax returns, capped at 5% of income. Tobacco manufacturers and retailers would face FDA regulation and marketing restrictions, gun dealers would face new transfer rules, and private employers (including those with 25-50 employees newly covered by family leave) would bear new wage and leave requirements. Health insurers would gain covered services but lose some customers to the public plan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, tobacco and gun industries, employers

drawbacks.text: The bill did not identify its funding: it set MediKids premiums to cover only 25% of estimated per-person costs and directed Treasury to merely 'propose a gradual schedule of progressive tax changes' later, leaving the full cost — potentially tens of billions annually as cohorts grew — unpaid on the record.

The bill bundled at least twelve unrelated titles spanning health care, taxes, wages, welfare, housing, foster care, juvenile justice, tobacco, and guns, which meant a member could not vote for the children's health provisions without also voting for the gun and tobacco provisions — a common reason omnibuses of this size stall.

It imposed new compliance costs on employers, extending family and medical leave mandates to firms with as few as 25 employees and requiring living wages on federal contracts, costs that small employers argued fall hardest on them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to children — near-universal health coverage, a higher wage floor, refundable tax credits, food assistance, and housing vouchers — are large and well-targeted to low-income families. The honest cost is fiscal: the bill promised coverage and programs while postponing the tax plan to pay for them, and its sheer breadth made it politically unwieldy even among potential allies.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to seven House committees the day it was introduced, got passed around among more than a dozen subcommittees over the next two months, and then sat with no hearings, markups, or floor action until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Representative George Miller of California and 26 other House Democrats introduced the bill on February 26, 2003.

The Speaker referred it to seven full committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Agriculture, the Judiciary, Government Reform, and Transportation and Infrastructure — for consideration of the provisions in each panel's jurisdiction.

Over the following weeks it was referred to more than a dozen subcommittees, including Health, Human Resources, Education Reform, and Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security; the last referral was on May 5, 2003.
That was the last action of any kind: the record shows no hearings, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
It gathered 97 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and gun dealers avoided the FDA regulation, gun show background checks, and magazine-import restrictions the bill contained; private insurers kept the children's coverage business that MediKids would have taken; and low-wage employers avoided the higher minimum wage, federal-contract living wage, and expanded leave mandates. Children and low-income families did not get the coverage or benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco and gun makers avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: All 98 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill died in committee without any recorded vote to show bipartisan positioning either way.

industries.note: The bill grants the FDA authority over tobacco products, restricts marketing and advertising aimed at youth, and adds access restrictions. The industry fought FDA tobacco authority for decades; its interest here ran against the children's health goal.

The bill extends Brady background checks to gun shows, requires child safety locks, bans imports of large-capacity ammunition feeding devices, restricts multiple handgun sales, and limits transfers to juveniles. The gun industry's interest ran against the bill's child-safety provisions.

MediKids creates a public insurer of last resort that automatically enrolls children, taking premiums away from private plans for families that drop employer coverage; meanwhile the bill imposes children's health accountability standards and mandatory childhood immunization coverage on plans regulated under ERISA and the Public Health Service Act. The industry's interest lay in keeping the public default plan off the table.

industries.industry: Child care providers and Head Start programs
industries.note: The bill funds child care provider retention grants and scholarships, facilities financing, higher reimbursement rates, and reserved Head Start funds for infants and toddlers, expanding both services and the paid workforce.

A graduated minimum wage increase, a poverty-level living wage on federal contracts, and extension of family and medical leave mandates to firms with 25 or more employees would raise labor costs, hitting employers of low-wage workers hardest.
MediKids covers prescription drugs and the bill mandates insurance coverage of childhood immunizations, creating paying customers among newly covered children.
